rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).

evidence_timeline.summary: Terminal mass-loss in massive stars is commonly reconstructed from observations of circumstellar interaction in core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe); however, such signatures can be easily missed depending on the phase when they appear. In this paper, we present a multi-wavelength study of SN\,2022yyz, a nearby CCSN selected by its luminous late-time mid-infrared (MIR) excess in NEOWISE at $> 500$ days after the discovery. Classified as a Type II SN at discovery, it reached a peak bolometric luminosity of $1.3^{+0.7}_{-0.4}\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$ before fading away with a light-curve drop at $\sim 300$ days. We present late-time HST/WFC3 ultraviolet (UV) imaging and Keck/LRIS spectroscopy at $\sim 1200$ days, which reveal clear signs of circumstellar-medium (CSM) interaction via a UV excess consistent with a strong MgII contribution and a flat-topped H$α$ profile. We show that the bolometric light curve and the late-time UV luminosity can be explained using a semi-analytic CSM interaction model involving a broken power-law density profile: with $\sim 2.7~M_\odot$ of nearby, dense CSM within a radius of $\sim 10^{16}$ cm surrounded by wind-like outer CSM with a mass-loss rate of $\sim 10^{-4} {\rm ~M_\odot~yr}^{-1}$. The broken density profile indicates $\gtrsim 100\times$ mass-loss rate enhancement starting a few hundred years before explosion, pointing to a possible common-envelope ejection in a binary system. Despite being overlooked for follow-up at such proximity, our results demonstrate that IR photometric selection methods provide a powerful way of mapping terminal mass-loss in massive stars - laying the groundwork for the Roman Space Telescope surveys.

publication_revisions.abstract: Terminal mass-loss in massive stars is commonly reconstructed from observations of circumstellar interaction in core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe); however, such signatures can be easily missed depending on the phase when they appear. In this paper, we present a multi-wavelength study of SN\,2022yyz, a nearby CCSN selected by its luminous late-time mid-infrared (MIR) excess in NEOWISE at $> 500$ days after the discovery. Classified as a Type II SN at discovery, it reached a peak bolometric luminosity of $1.3^{+0.7}_{-0.4}\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$ before fading away with a light-curve drop at $\sim 300$ days. We present late-time HST/WFC3 ultraviolet (UV) imaging and Keck/LRIS spectroscopy at $\sim 1200$ days, which reveal clear signs of circumstellar-medium (CSM) interaction via a UV excess consistent with a strong MgII contribution and a flat-topped H$α$ profile. We show that the bolometric light curve and the late-time UV luminosity can be explained using a semi-analytic CSM interaction model involving a broken power-law density profile: with $\sim 2.7~M_\odot$ of nearby, dense CSM within a radius of $\sim 10^{16}$ cm surrounded by wind-like outer CSM with a mass-loss rate of $\sim 10^{-4} {\rm ~M_\odot~yr}^{-1}$. The broken density profile indicates $\gtrsim 100\times$ mass-loss rate enhancement starting a few hundred years before explosion, pointing to a possible common-envelope ejection in a binary system. Despite being overlooked for follow-up at such proximity, our results demonstrate that IR photometric selection methods provide a powerful way of mapping terminal mass-loss in massive stars - laying the groundwork for the Roman Space Telescope surveys.

rules.classification: Spectroscopic classes and alert or messenger labels are different definitions and are not compared; two active classes differ when neither label refines the other (for example 'SN Ia' and 'SN Ia-91T' agree); an earlier value from the same provider is a revision.
rules.host: Two proposed hosts agree when their names match after case and spacing are ignored or one name is among the other's NED cross-identifications; otherwise they are an identity ambiguity. Association probabilities are not computed.
rules.photometry: Only exactly compatible photometry (same epoch, band, system, method, calibration and direct/difference state, two or more providers) is compared. The limiting magnitude or flux that a provider reports alongside a detection is that epoch's detection threshold, not a non-detection, and is not compared with the detection; a detection brighter than another provider's non-detection limit at the same epoch is a status conflict. A group is listed only when it is still inconsistent under these rules; at most 10 groups per event, most significant first.
rules.position: Two positions with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they are more than 2 arcsec apart; when one states an error radius, the separation is compared with 3 times that radius.
rules.redshift: Two redshifts with no stated uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 0.005 (about 1,500 km/s); transient and host redshifts are different definitions and are listed, not compared; host redshifts of differently named hosts are an identity ambiguity.
rules.revision: A retracted row, or a superseded row of the same provider whose value differs beyond the property's rule, is a revision or retraction; a revision within the rule is consistent; the earlier value stays visible.
rules.sigma: Two values that both state an uncertainty are inconsistent when they differ by more than 3 combined standard deviations (uncertainties added in quadrature; a stated position error radius is treated as one standard deviation).
